answer: An in-place runtime upgrade can address a modernization problem when the main driver is lifecycle or security support (for example, a documented unsupported runtime or dependency), and the existing APIs and persisted state need not move, so one authoritative data writer can be preserved. It remains conditional: the required runtime/library combination must run, old data encoding must stay readable, and mixed-version releases must preserve externally required behavior, backed by contract tests and a reversible upgrade path. If those compatibility or behavior-preservation conditions fail, or the real problem requires a distinct capability/state owner or independent deployment, an in-place upgrade is contraindicated; moving a deployment boundary is not equivalent to transferring data ownership.
